extracted.intended_audience: general readers of humorous travel literature; tourists and travelers
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th‑century humorous travelogue satirizing guides, dramatic criticism, tourist behavior, and credulous historical claims; the text mixes travel description with comic instruction on how to behave as a tourist. Useful for studying humor, satire, and traveler–guide interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance/house as a measure of success
rubrics_metrics.description: “Some sixty thousand persons were present, and but for the fact that the streets were almost impassable, it is fair to presume that the house would have been full.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics treat crowd size and whether the house is full (or would have been) as evidence of a performance's success or public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management and facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: “The late repairs and decorations add both to the comeliness and the comfort of the Coliseum. The new cushions are a great improvement upon the hard marble seats we have been so long accustomed to. The present management deserve well of the public.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise (or blame) management for investments in comfort, repairs, decorations and restoration; such improvements factor into the critic's overall judgment of the enterprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance quality — technique and choreography
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews focus on technical execution: e.g., “The elder of the two young gentlemen handled his weapon with a grace that marked the possession of extraordinary talent. His feint of thrusting, followed instantly by a happily delivered blow ... he was not thoroughly up in the backhanded stroke, but ... practice would have overcome this defect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics evaluate individual technique, note specific defects (with expectation that practice will correct them), and use concrete stage-action descriptions to support praise or criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional decorum and audience appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: “We suggest that such exhibitions interfere with the decorum which should be preserved during the performances, and are highly improper in the presence of the Emperor.” (referring to a mother screaming and fainting)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether audience reactions (screaming, fainting, rowdiness) are appropriate to the occasion and context; such behavior can detract from the performance and merit admonition in a review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star's professionalism and stage manners
rubrics_metrics.description: “If he has a fault ... it is that of glancing at the audience, in the midst of the most exciting moments ... pausing in a fight to bow when bouquets are thrown to him is also in bad taste ... Such levity is proper enough in the provinces ... but it ill suits the dignity of the metropolis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actors are judged not only on skill but on professional decorum — avoiding self‑seeking gestures, excessive adulation‑seeking, or inappropriate levity for the genre or venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's tone: fair severity and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: “We mean them solely for his benefit. All who know us are aware that although we are at times justly severe upon tigers and martyrs, we never intentionally offend gladiators.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic should be able to be sharply observant and witty while remaining, in tone, consciously fair and not malicious; humor in criticism is acceptable when framed as constructive or good‑natured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program variety and advertised changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Playbill: “Material change of programme every evening.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Managers are credited for offering variety and for managing expectations when programmes change; advertised promises (e.g., nightly changes) are an aspect of evaluating the offering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, order, and crowd control
rubrics_metrics.description: Playbill: “An efficient police force will be on hand to preserve order and keep the wild beasts from leaping the railings and discommoding the audience.” Critic: admonishes police to stop gallery boys from throwing peanuts and derisive remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety measures and effective crowd control are part of event evaluation; failure to maintain order or protect spectators (or performers) is criticism‑worthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide accuracy and correct attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated comic scenario where guides attribute every great work to Michael Angelo: e.g., the guide being asked “By Michael Angelo?” about statues and obelisks long before Michelangelo's time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides should avoid facile or erroneous attributions; accuracy of history, chronology, and authorship is a core standard for evaluating a guide's competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guide presentation and language competence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Guides know about enough English to tangle every thing up so that a man can make neither head or tail of it. They know their story by heart--the history of every statue... and tell it as a parrot would--and if you interrupt, and throw them off the track, they have to go back and begin over again.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate guides on clarity, ability to handle interruptions/questions, language skills, and whether they merely parrot memorized text versus engaging knowledgeably with tourists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactic for dealing with showy guides: feigned indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: Travelers deliberately show “impassible faces and stupid indifference” to exhaust a guide's desire for admiration; an especially effective question is: “Is--is he dead?” which ‘conquers the serenest of them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is prescriptive tourist behavior: to counter over‑enthusiastic guides, display indifference and ask naive or deflating questions to interrupt their performance; presented as a comic but practical technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward miraculous or extraordinary relic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary on Rev. Neligan's reports: e.g., tongues and hearts found whole after a century, blood dropping from a heart — “This author puts my credulity on its mettle ... I would gladly change my unbelief for Neligan's faith.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt critical scrutiny toward extraordinary historical or hagiographic claims; don't accept miraculous statements uncritically — require plausible evidence and note when learned authors assert unlikely wonders.
